concepts.title: Logging
concepts.description: The logging module replaces scattered print() calls with a leveled, filterable, configurable system for recording what a program is doing, which you need once code runs somewhere you can't watch it.
learningObjectives: Explain why print() debugging breaks down once code runs in production or spans multiple modules.
Order the five standard logging levels and describe what each is actually meant to communicate.
Configure basic logging output with logging.basicConfig and obtain a per-module logger with logging.getLogger(__name__).
Describe the roles of loggers, handlers, and formatters, and explain how a level acts as a filter, not a label.
Predict whether a given log call will actually produce visible output based on the configured level.

sections.heading: Why print() Doesn't Scale
sections.body: `print()` is the natural first tool for finding out what a program is doing, and for a five-line script it's fine. In a larger codebase it falls short: `print()` has no concept of severity, so a message that just confirms normal progress looks identical to one reporting a failure. Both are lines of text on stdout. It has no built-in timestamp, no indication of which module or function produced it, and no way to turn it off selectively. If you've sprinkled twenty `print()` calls across a module while chasing a bug, the only way to quiet them again is to go back and delete or comment out every single one, and it's easy to miss one, or to need it again three days later. Worse, in a deployed service, `print()` output usually just vanishes into whatever swallowed stdout, or mixes with everything else with no way to filter 'only show me warnings from the payment module.' Logging attaches a level, a source, and a timestamp to each message, and lets you decide *later*, without touching the call sites, how verbose to be and where the output should go.

sections.heading: The Five Levels, and What Each Is For
sections.body:
Python's logging module defines five standard severity levels, each with a numeric value that determines an ordering: `DEBUG` (10), `INFO` (20), `WARNING` (30), `ERROR` (40), `CRITICAL` (50). Knowing the ordering matters less than knowing what each one is *for*:

- **DEBUG**: fine-grained diagnostic detail useful while actively developing or investigating: variable values, which branch was taken, how many items were processed. Too noisy to leave on in normal production use.
- **INFO**: confirmation that things are working as expected: `"Server started on port 8000"`, `"Processed 42 records"`. The normal, healthy heartbeat of a running program.
- **WARNING**: something unexpected happened, or a potential problem was noticed, but the program can still carry on: a deprecated function was called, a retry was needed, a config value fell back to a default.
- **ERROR**: a problem. A specific operation failed and did not complete as intended, though the program as a whole may still be running (e.g. one request out of many failed).
- **CRITICAL**: a serious error suggesting the *program itself* may be unable to continue: out of disk space, a corrupted essential file, an unrecoverable startup failure.

The numeric ordering is what makes filtering possible: a logger or handler configured with a minimum level only lets through messages *at or above* that level. Set the threshold to `WARNING`, and every `DEBUG` and `INFO` call is dropped without an error. That's what you want in production, and it's also why an `info()` call you expected to see may never show up.

sections.heading: Getting Started: basicConfig and Per-Module Loggers
sections.body:
The fastest way to get useful output is `logging.basicConfig()`, called once, early, ideally near your program's entry point:

```python
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
)
```

This sets up a reasonable default: a handler that writes to the console (to stderr, not stdout), a formatter that includes a timestamp, the level name, and the logger's name, and a minimum level of `INFO`. One thing to watch for: `basicConfig()` only has an effect the *first* time it's called with a handler not already configured. Calling it again later in the same process, expecting to change the level, is a no-op unless you pass `force=True`. It comes up often in notebooks and test suites, where something may already have configured logging.

Instead of calling module-level functions like `logging.info(...)` (which all log through the single root logger, and call `basicConfig()` for you if it has no handlers), the standard idiom is to get a logger named after the current module: `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)`. Passing `__name__` names the logger after the module's fully qualified dotted path (e.g. `myapp.utils.orders`), so every log record it produces reports where it came from, and, more importantly for larger projects, lets you dial the verbosity of one module up or down later without touching a call site.

sections.heading: Loggers, Handlers, and Formatters
sections.body:
Three pieces cover almost everything you'll need day to day:

- **Logger**: the object your code calls (`logger.debug(...)`, `logger.info(...)`, etc.). It has a name and a minimum level (its own, or inherited from its parent), and it's the first gate a message passes through. If the message's level is below the logger's level, processing stops right there.
- **Handler**: decides *where* a message that made it past the logger's filter goes: the console (`StreamHandler`), a file (`FileHandler`), a network service, and so on. A handler has its *own* level too, which is a second, independent gate: a message must clear both the logger's level and the handler's level to be emitted. This is why a message can sometimes vanish even though the logger's level looks low enough. A stricter handler further down the pipeline can still be filtering it out.
- **Formatter**: decides what the final output line looks like: which fields (timestamp, level, logger name, message) appear and in what format.

`basicConfig()` is a convenience that wires up one root-level handler and formatter for you in a single call, which is enough for most small-to-medium projects. The full hierarchy (multiple handlers per logger, propagation to parent loggers, per-handler levels different from the logger's own level) is there when you need it (e.g. writing DEBUG detail to a file while only showing WARNING and above on the console), but you don't need to learn it up front.

examples.title: From print() to a Configured Logger
examples.code:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def process_order(order_id):
    logger.info("Processing order %s", order_id)
    if order_id < 0:
        logger.error("Invalid order id: %s", order_id)
        return
    logger.debug("Order %s passed validation", order_id)  # filtered out -- level is INFO
    logger.info("Order %s processed successfully", order_id)

process_order(42)
process_order(-1)
examples.explanation: Because `basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)` sets the threshold to INFO, the `logger.debug(...)` call is dropped, DEBUG (10) is below INFO (20), while both `info()` and `error()` calls are shown, each with a timestamp and the logger's name (`__main__` in a script run) automatically prepended by the formatter. The log calls use `%s` placeholders with `order_id` passed as a separate argument, rather than an f-string like `f"Processing order {order_id}"`. Logging builds the final message string only if a handler emits it, so a filtered-out call skips the formatting, while an f-string is built every time. Only the formatting is deferred: Python still evaluates the arguments, so `logger.debug("%s", expensive_computation())` runs `expensive_computation()` even when DEBUG is off. Guard a call like that with `if logger.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG):`.

examples.title: Per-Module Verbosity and Quieting a Noisy Library
examples.code:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING, format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")

db_logger = logging.getLogger("myapp.database")
api_logger = logging.getLogger("myapp.api")

db_logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)   # debugging the database layer right now

db_logger.debug("Opening connection pool")     # shown -- db_logger's own level is DEBUG
api_logger.debug("Preparing request headers")  # not shown -- api_logger has no override, inherits WARNING

# keep a chatty third-party library at WARNING even if the root level is lowered later
logging.getLogger("urllib3").setLevel(logging.WARNING)
examples.explanation: Each call to `logging.getLogger(name)` with the same string returns the *same* logger object every time, so `db_logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)` changes that one named logger's threshold without touching anything else. `api_logger` never had its own level set, so it falls back to the effective level it inherits (WARNING, from the root logger configured by `basicConfig`), which is why its `debug()` call produces nothing. This is what naming loggers after modules buys you: you can turn up verbosity for the module you're investigating, leave everything else quiet, and do it all without editing application code. The database record still reaches the console even though the root logger is at WARNING: a record is checked against the level of the logger it was logged on, then handed to ancestor *handlers*, without consulting the ancestor loggers' levels. The last line shows the same trick applied to a third-party library's logger by name, a common way to quiet noisy dependencies without losing your own app's messages.

misconceptions.description: logging.info("...") is basically just a fancier print() -- the two are interchangeable, and it doesn't really matter which one you reach for.
misconceptions.clarification: Both can end up printing text, but logging calls carry a severity level, so the same call site can be shown during development and silenced in production (or vice versa) by changing one configuration line, with no other code changes. logging output can include timestamps and the originating module automatically, can be redirected to a file, a network service, or multiple destinations at once via handlers, and can be filtered per-module rather than all-or-nothing. print() has none of that. It always goes to stdout, always shows, and always looks identical regardless of how important the message is. print() is fine for a throwaway check, or for a command-line tool's own output; diagnostics that stay in the code belong in logging.

misconceptions.description: Setting a logger's level to something 'higher,' like WARNING instead of INFO, makes it produce more output, since WARNING sounds like a bigger deal.
misconceptions.clarification: It's the opposite, and the numeric values make the mechanism clear: DEBUG=10, INFO=20, WARNING=30, ERROR=40, CRITICAL=50. A logger's level is a *minimum threshold*. Only messages at that level or higher pass through. Raising the threshold from INFO to WARNING means DEBUG and INFO calls now fall below the bar and get dropped, leaving *only* WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL. Strictly less output, not more. 'Higher level' means 'stricter filter, more severe messages only,' not 'more verbose.' The most verbose setting is the *lowest* level, DEBUG, since it lets everything through.

exercises.prompt: Given this setup, which of the four log calls actually produce visible output?
exercises.code:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

logger.debug("starting up")
logger.info("connected to database")
logger.warning("cache miss, falling back to database")
logger.error("failed to save record")
hints: The level passed to basicConfig sets a minimum threshold, not a label for one specific kind of message.
Recall the numeric ordering: DEBUG=10, INFO=20, WARNING=30, ERROR=40, CRITICAL=50. Which of these four calls are at or above WARNING (30)?
Two of the four calls are below the configured threshold and are dropped. Not an error, just no output at all for those lines.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Only the warning() and error() calls print anything: 'WARNING: cache miss, falling back to database' and 'ERROR: failed to save record'. The debug() and info() calls are below the configured WARNING threshold (30), so they're filtered out and produce no output whatsoever.
exercises.solutionExplanation: basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING) sets the root logger's threshold to 30. logger.debug() is level 10 and logger.info() is level 20. Both below 30, so both are dropped before any formatting or output happens. logger.warning() is 30 and logger.error() is 40, both at or above the threshold, so both pass through and get formatted and printed. When a log message doesn't show up, check the configured threshold first.

exercises.prompt: A teammate added logging calls to their script expecting to see startup and progress messages, but running it produces no output at all -- not even an error. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def main():
    logger.info("Starting up")
    for i in range(3):
        logger.info("Processing item %s", i)
    logger.info("Done")

main()
hints: The code never calls logging.basicConfig() anywhere. What level does a logger have by default without any configuration?
Without any configuration, the root logger's level defaults to WARNING, and every logger.info() call here is below that threshold.
You need one call, before these info() calls run, that sets up a handler and lowers the effective minimum level to INFO or below.
exercises.solutionCode:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def main():
    logger.info("Starting up")
    for i in range(3):
        logger.info("Processing item %s", i)
    logger.info("Done")

main()
exercises.solutionExplanation: With no call to basicConfig() (or any other handler configuration) anywhere in the process, the root logger has no handlers attached and its level defaults to WARNING. (A warning or error would still appear, because logging has a last-resort handler that prints WARNING and above to stderr.) Every logger.info() call here is level 20, below that default threshold of 30, so each one is dropped. There's no error because filtering a message below the threshold is normal behavior, not a failure. Adding logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) before any info() calls run attaches a console handler and lowers the effective minimum level to INFO, which is low enough to let all of these calls through.

assessments.prompt: A logger is configured with `logger.setLevel(logging.ERROR)`, and its handler is separately configured with `handler.setLevel(logging.WARNING)`. If the code calls `logger.warning("low disk space")`, what happens?
options: It is shown twice, once for each level check that passes.
It is shown, because the handler's level (WARNING) is low enough to allow it.
It raises a ValueError because the logger and handler levels don't match.
It is not shown, because the logger's own level (ERROR) already filters it out before the handler is ever consulted.
assessments.explanation: A message has to clear the logger's own level first. That's the first gate. logger.warning() produces a WARNING (30) level record, but the logger's threshold is ERROR (40), so the message is filtered out immediately, before it's ever passed along to any handler. The handler's more permissive WARNING threshold is irrelevant here because the message never reaches the handler at all. The logger's level and the handler's level are independent filters, and a message must pass both.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a teammate who has only ever used print() why they should switch to the logging module for a project that's about to be deployed, and what logging.getLogger(__name__) buys them over calling logging.info() directly.
assessments.modelAnswer: print() has no concept of severity, no timestamps by default, and no way to selectively silence it. Every print() call always produces output, always goes to stdout, and looks identical whether it's a routine status update or a sign of trouble. Once code runs somewhere you can't just sit and watch (a deployed service, a scheduled job, another developer's machine), that undifferentiated stream is a problem: you either see everything, including noise you don't care about, or you go back and manually delete print() calls, which is easy to get wrong and annoying to undo later. logging solves this by attaching a severity level (DEBUG through CRITICAL) to every message and letting you set a threshold. Change one configuration line, and DEBUG-level noise disappears from production while WARNING and above still show, with zero changes to the call sites themselves. As for logging.getLogger(__name__): calling logging.info() uses the single shared root logger, so every part of the program looks the same in the logs and you can't turn one module's verbosity up or down independently. Passing __name__ names the logger after that specific module's dotted path, so log records report where they came from, and, you can later say 'set myapp.database to DEBUG, leave everything else at WARNING' while actively investigating one part of the system, without touching a single log call anywhere in the code.

assessments.prompt:
```python
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING)
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)   # trying to lower the level afterward

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.debug("checking cache")
```
What happens?
options: Nothing is printed, but only because logger.debug() requires an explicit handler argument to work at all
Nothing is printed -- the second basicConfig() call is a no-op
It raises an error, since basicConfig() can only ever be called once per program
"checking cache" is printed, since the second basicConfig() call successfully lowers the level to DEBUG
assessments.explanation: basicConfig() only has an effect the first time it's called with no handler already configured. Once the first call has set one up, later calls (without passing force=True) are ignored, even though they don't raise any error. So the effective level stays WARNING (30) from the first call, and logger.debug() (level 10) is still below that threshold and gets filtered out, printing nothing. It often shows up in notebooks or test suites, where basicConfig() may already have run.

assessments.prompt:
```python
import logging

logger_a = logging.getLogger("myapp.jobs")
logger_a.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

logger_b = logging.getLogger("myapp.jobs")   # same name, requested elsewhere in the code

print(logger_a is logger_b)
print(logger_b.level == logging.DEBUG)
```
What gets printed?
options: True then True
False then False
False then True
True then False
assessments.explanation: `logging.getLogger(name)` returns the exact same logger object every time it's called with the same name string. There's no per-call duplication. So `logger_a` and `logger_b`, despite being obtained from two separate calls (potentially in two different parts of a codebase), are the same object in memory: `logger_a is logger_b` is `True`. Since `logger_b` is that same object, the level set via `logger_a.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)` is already reflected on it. `logger_b.level == logging.DEBUG` is also `True`. This is why `logging.getLogger(__name__)` is a safe, idiomatic pattern to call repeatedly throughout a module without worrying about creating redundant loggers.

concepts.title: Testing with pytest
concepts.description: pytest lets you write tests as plain functions with plain assert statements, then discovers and runs them, so regressions are caught without manual spot-checking.
learningObjectives: Explain why an automated test suite catches regressions that manual testing and code review routinely miss.
Write pytest tests using plain assert statements, without any special assertion methods.
Apply pytest's discovery conventions to explain why a given test would or would not be picked up and run.
Use a pytest fixture to share setup logic across multiple tests without duplicating code.
Identify the qualities of a well-written test: one behavior per test, a descriptive name, and independence from other tests.

sections.heading: What Automated Tests Catch
sections.body: Manually re-checking every code path by hand (click through the app, try a few inputs, eyeball the output) works for a while, but it doesn't scale: the number of code paths worth checking grows every time you add a feature, while the amount of time and patience you have for re-checking old ones by hand stays roughly flat. So old behavior breaks and nobody notices until a user hits it. An automated test suite reruns all of those checks in seconds. It catches **regressions**, changes that accidentally break something that used to work, often before a human ever sees the breakage, and it **documents expected behavior** in a form that's verified to be true, unlike a comment or a wiki page that can go stale. It also makes refactoring safer: you restructure the code, rerun the suite, and find out within seconds if covered behavior changed.

sections.heading: pytest's Philosophy: Plain assert
sections.body:
Python's built-in `unittest` framework requires learning a family of special assertion methods (`self.assertEqual(a, b)`, `self.assertTrue(x)`, `self.assertIn(x, y)`, and dozens more), each producing its own particular failure message. pytest takes a different approach: you just write ordinary `assert` statements, and pytest rewrites them under the hood (via its "assertion rewriting" import hook) to produce a detailed failure report without any special method:

```python
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

def test_add():
    assert add(2, 3) == 5
```

If that assertion fails (say `add` had a bug and returned 6), pytest doesn't just say "assertion failed"; it shows the values it computed on both sides of the comparison in the terminal output. If you can write an `if` condition, you already know most of what you need to write a pytest test.

sections.heading: Test Discovery: Conventions pytest Relies On
sections.body: pytest doesn't need you to register tests anywhere. It finds them automatically by walking your project's directories and applying a small set of naming conventions: files named `test_*.py` or `*_test.py`, functions inside them whose names start with `test` (by convention `test_*`), and, if you group tests in classes, classes named `Test*` containing such methods. The drawback is that a function with good test logic but the wrong name will never be run, with no warning and no error. Typical cases are a name like `check_total`, a typo like `tset_total`, or a capitalized `Test_total` on a function (the prefix is case-sensitive). If a test you wrote doesn't appear in the count, run `pytest --collect-only` to see what was collected.

sections.heading: Fixtures: Shared Setup and Teardown
sections.body:
Many tests need some shared setup (a fresh object to test against, a temporary file, a database connection), and often the same setup across several tests. `unittest` handles this with `setUp()`/`tearDown()` methods tied to a test class. pytest's answer is **fixtures**: a function decorated with `@pytest.fixture` that any test can request by naming it as a parameter:

```python
import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def shopping_cart():
    cart = []
    yield cart          # this value is handed to the test
    cart.clear()         # runs after the test finishes -- teardown

def test_cart_starts_empty(shopping_cart):
    assert shopping_cart == []

def test_adding_item_increases_length(shopping_cart):
    shopping_cart.append("apple")
    assert len(shopping_cart) == 1
```

pytest matches the parameter name `shopping_cart` in each test function to the fixture of the same name, calls the fixture, and hands the test whatever value the fixture produced before its `yield`. Anything written *after* `yield` runs as teardown, once the test using it has finished, whether it passed or failed. By default, a fixture reruns for every test that requests it, so `test_cart_starts_empty` and `test_adding_item_increases_length` each get their own independent, empty list. Appending in one test has no effect on the other. Fixtures can also be scoped to run once per module or per test session, which is useful when setup is slow (starting a database, say), but the default covers most needs.

sections.heading: What Makes a Good Test
sections.body: A few habits keep a test suite useful. **Test one behavior per test**. A test named `test_withdraw` that also happens to check deposits, error handling, and interest calculation makes it hard to tell, from a failure, what broke. **Name tests descriptively, by behavior, not by number**. `test_withdraw_raises_when_balance_insufficient` tells you immediately what broke when it fails; `test_3` tells you nothing without opening the file. **Keep tests independent of each other**. A test shouldn't depend on another test having run first (or in a particular order), since you'll want to run one test alone while debugging, and plugins that shuffle tests or run them in parallel (`pytest-randomly`, `pytest-xdist`) change the order. And **keep tests fast**. People stop running a slow suite. If one expensive setup step dominates, give that fixture a broader scope.

examples.title: A Failing Test and What pytest Reports
examples.code:
def calculate_discount(price, percent_off):
    return price - (price * percent_off / 100)

def test_calculate_discount():
    assert calculate_discount(100, 20) == 90

# Running `pytest` on this file produces:
#
#     def test_calculate_discount():
# >       assert calculate_discount(100, 20) == 90
# E       assert 80.0 == 90
# E        +  where 80.0 = calculate_discount(100, 20)
#
# pytest shows the ACTUAL computed value (80.0) right next to the
# expected one (90) -- no assertEqual() or custom message needed.
examples.explanation: The bug here is in the test: taking 20% off of 100 should leave 80, not 90, so the expected value is wrong. (A failing test isn't always the code's fault.) Look at the *output*: pytest's assertion rewriting inspects the failed `assert` statement and shows you both sides of the `==` comparison with their runtime values, plus the call that produced 80.0, with no `self.assertEqual(...)` and no custom message.

examples.title: A Fixture Shared Across Independent Tests
examples.explanation: Both tests request the `empty_cart` fixture by naming it as a parameter, and pytest calls the fixture function fresh for each test that requests it. The default fixture scope is `"function"`, meaning one independent call per test function. `test_first` appends `"apple"` to *its own* list produced by that call, and when `test_first` finishes, the fixture's teardown (`cart.clear()`, after the `yield`) runs. When `test_second` starts, pytest calls the fixture function again from scratch, producing a brand-new empty list. So `test_second` starts from zero, unaffected by whatever `test_first` did. That independence is what makes tests safe to run in any order, or individually while debugging.

misconceptions.description: pytest requires special assertion methods like unittest's assertEqual/assertTrue, and plain assert statements won't give you a useful failure message.
misconceptions.clarification: pytest rewrites plain assert statements at import time (its assertion rewriting hook) so that ordinary Python assert expressions produce rich, introspected failure output, showing the runtime values on both sides of a comparison, without any special method. unittest's assert* method zoo exists mostly because plain assert in that older framework doesn't get this treatment; pytest removed the need for it.

misconceptions.description: Any function containing test-like logic, as long as it lives inside a file in a 'tests' folder, will automatically be picked up and run by pytest.
misconceptions.clarification: pytest's discovery is based on naming conventions, not folder location alone: the file generally needs to match test_*.py or *_test.py, and the function itself needs to be named test_* (or be a test_* method inside a Test*-named class). A helper function sitting in a correctly-named test file, but itself named e.g. check_totals() instead of test_totals(), is skipped (not an error, just never collected or run), which is one of the most common 'why isn't this test running' surprises for people new to the framework.
misconceptions.fact: pytest's discovery is based on naming conventions, not folder location alone: the file generally needs to match test_*.py or *_test.py, and the function itself needs to be named test_* (or be a test_* method inside a Test*-named class).

exercises.prompt: A developer wrote this test to check that discount calculation works, but running `pytest` on this file reports "no tests ran," not a failure. The discount function itself is correct. Find and fix the bug that's preventing pytest from running the test.
hints: pytest discovers tests by name, not by what the function's body does. Look closely at the test function's name.
Functions pytest treats as tests must be named starting with test_. Does check_calculate_discount() match that pattern?
Rename the function so pytest collects it. The run should then report one passing test.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The reason pytest reports "no tests ran" instead of a failure is that check_calculate_discount doesn't match pytest's test_* discovery convention, so pytest never collects it. Renaming it to test_calculate_discount makes pytest collect and run it, and it passes: 20% off 100 is 80. The danger of this bug is that a suite with other, correctly named tests would still show green, with this check missing. Keep an eye on the collected count, and break the code on purpose once to confirm a new test can fail.

exercises.prompt: Running this file with `pytest -s` (so print output is shown), what does each print() call output, given that both test functions request the same fixture?
hints: A fixture function's body runs again, fresh, every time a NEW test requests it, unless the fixture is given a broader scope than the default.
The default fixture scope is 'function', meaning one fresh call per test function that requests it.
test_two never sees anything test_one appended. It gets its own brand-new empty list from a fresh call to counter_list().
exercises.expectedAnswer: test_one prints 2 (after appending 'a' and 'b'). test_two prints 0, because it gets a completely separate, freshly-created empty list from its own independent call to the fixture. The default function scope means the fixture reruns per test, with no shared state between them.
exercises.solutionExplanation: @pytest.fixture with no scope argument defaults to scope="function", meaning pytest calls counter_list() fresh, once per test function that requests it as a parameter. test_one gets its own list, appends two items to it, and prints its length: 2. When test_two runs, pytest calls counter_list() again from scratch, a brand new, empty items list, completely independent of whatever test_one did to its own list. So test_two prints 0. If the two tests needed to share state, that would require a broader fixture scope (like "module" or "session"), an uncommon choice, because sharing mutable state between tests tends to make them harder to run independently or in any order.

assessments.prompt: A test suite has a file named `checkout_tests.py` containing a function named `test_total_with_tax()`. Running plain `pytest` in the project root, what happens?
options: The test runs normally, since the function name follows the test_* convention.
The test runs, but pytest issues a warning about the file naming.
The test is not discovered, since the file name doesn't match pytest's default test_*.py or *_test.py discovery pattern.
pytest raises an ImportError because the file name is invalid.
assessments.explanation: pytest's default discovery requires BOTH the file name and the function name to match its conventions. checkout_tests.py matches neither test_*.py nor *_test.py (it would need to be named e.g. test_checkout.py or checkout_test.py), so pytest never even opens this file looking for tests, regardless of what's inside it or how well-named the function is. Renaming the function alone (as in the “The test runs normally, since the function…” option) doesn't help if the containing file itself isn't discovered. There's no ImportError or warning involved (“pytest raises an ImportError because the file…” and “The test runs, but pytest issues…”). Non-matching files are skipped without any message.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: "We already review every pull request by hand, so I don't see what automated tests add." Explain what a test suite catches that manual code review typically does not, and why plain assert statements in pytest are enough without a special assertion API.
assessments.modelAnswer: Code review is good at catching things a human reading the diff can reason about (unclear logic, missing edge-case handling, style issues), but it doesn't re-execute the rest of the codebase to confirm that a change didn't break some unrelated behavior three modules away that the reviewer never looked at and has no reason to suspect. An automated test suite does that, every time, in seconds: it re-verifies previously-working behavior on every change, which is how regressions get caught. It also documents expected behavior in a form that is checked on every run, unlike a comment or design doc that can drift out of date. As for plain assert: pytest rewrites assert statements at import time so that a plain `assert calculate_total(cart) == 42` produces a detailed report showing the computed value versus the expected one, without needing a dedicated method like assertEqual(). If you can write a boolean condition, you can write a pytest test, with no separate assertion vocabulary to learn.

assessments.prompt:
```python
import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def resource():
    print("setup")
    yield "value"
    print("teardown")

def test_uses_resource(resource):
    print("test body")
    assert False   # deliberately failing
```
What gets printed, and does the fixture's teardown still run despite the test failing?
options: setup / test body -- teardown never runs, since the test raised before reaching it
setup / teardown / test body -- pytest runs teardown before the test body for safety
setup / test body / teardown -- and the test is still reported as failed
setup / test body -- and the process crashes with an unhandled AssertionError before pytest can report anything
assessments.explanation: A fixture's teardown code (everything after `yield`) is guaranteed to run once the test using it finishes, regardless of whether that test passed or failed. The same guarantee applies to `finally` and context managers. So even though `assert False` causes `test_uses_resource` to fail, pytest still resumes the `resource` fixture after the test concludes, running `print("teardown")` before moving on. The test is correctly reported as a failure. The guaranteed teardown doesn't change or hide that outcome, it just ensures cleanup code isn't skipped because of it.

assessments.prompt: A test named `test_checkout` asserts five different things in one function: the total is calculated correctly, inventory is decremented, a confirmation email object is created, a discount code is applied correctly, and an invalid discount code raises an error. It fails. What's the most accurate criticism?
options: Bundling five distinct behaviors into one test makes it hard to tell, from the failure alone, which of the five things actually broke
The test should be renamed test_1 through test_5 instead of using one descriptive name
Nothing is wrong with it -- as long as every assertion eventually runs, one test function covering many behaviors is always the most efficient structure
pytest refuses to execute a test function containing more than one assert statement
assessments.explanation: One of the core qualities of a good test is checking one behavior per test. When a test this broad fails, its name doesn't say which of five unrelated behaviors broke, and because the first failing assert stops the test, the remaining checks never run. Splitting it into five focused, descriptively-named tests (like `test_checkout_calculates_total_correctly`, `test_checkout_rejects_invalid_discount_code`, and so on) means a failure immediately tells you what broke, just from the test's name. The “pytest refuses to execute a test function…” option is false. Pytest has no restriction on the number of assert statements per test function; the problem is readability.

concepts.title: Debugging
concepts.description: Debugging as a process: reading a traceback, using pdb/breakpoint() to inspect live state, and knowing when print-debugging helps and when it wastes time.
learningObjectives: Read a Python traceback bottom-up to identify the actual exception and trace the call stack that led to it.
Use breakpoint() and basic pdb commands to pause execution and inspect live variable state.
Judge when print-debugging is a reasonable quick tool versus when it wastes more time than it saves.
Apply a general debugging workflow: reproduce reliably, narrow down, form a hypothesis, verify.
Distinguish where an exception was raised from where the root cause of the bug actually lives.

sections.heading: Reading a Traceback Bottom-Up
sections.body: A Python traceback lists, top to bottom, the chain of calls that led to an exception, starting from the outermost call and descending into deeper and deeper function calls, ending with the line that raised the error and the exception itself. Make a habit of **reading from the bottom up**: the very last line names the exception type and its message. That's the error, and it's usually the fastest place to start understanding what went wrong. Each frame above it, read upward, is one more level out in the call stack: the function that called the function that eventually failed, and so on, up to wherever your program's execution began. Beginners often start from the top, but that line is usually the least useful. It tells you the program started running, which you already knew.

sections.heading: The Bottom Tells You Where, Not Always Why
sections.body: The last frame tells you *where* the exception was raised, but that is not always *where the bug is*. A function three calls deep might raise a `TypeError` because it received `None` where it expected a number. But the mistake might be several frames further up the stack, in whatever code passed `None` in the first place, perhaps because an earlier lookup failed and returned `None` without anyone checking for it. So start at the bottom to understand *what* went wrong and *where* it blew up, then walk upward through the frames above it to trace *why*: which caller supplied the bad value, and where that value came from. Fixing the crash site alone sometimes just moves the same underlying problem one level over.

sections.heading: pdb and breakpoint(): Stepping Into the Program
sections.body:
Since Python 3.7, the built-in `breakpoint()` function drops you into an interactive debugger (`pdb` by default) at the line where it's called, with no import:

```python
def calculate_total(items):
    subtotal = sum(item.price for item in items)
    breakpoint()   # execution pauses here
    discount = apply_discount(subtotal)
    return subtotal - discount
```

Once paused, a handful of commands cover most needs: `n` (next line, staying in the current function), `s` (step, following execution *into* a function call), `c` (continue running until the next breakpoint or the program ends), `l` (list the surrounding source code), `p <expr>` or `pp <expr>` (print, or pretty-print, the value of any expression, including local variables), and `q` (quit the debugger). Compared with print-debugging, you can inspect any variable in scope, including ones you didn't think to print in advance, and step through conditionally-reached code without re-running the program for each new question.

sections.heading: When print-Debugging Is Fine, and When It Wastes Time
sections.body: For a short, deterministic script where you have a specific, narrow question ("what value does this variable have right here?"), adding one `print()` and rerunning is often faster than starting an interactive session. Print-debugging starts wasting time once any of these apply: the bug requires several rounds of edit-rerun-inspect, each one costing a full program restart; the interesting moment is deep inside a loop or recursive call where you'd need to print dozens of times or add conditional print logic just to catch the right iteration; or you don't yet know *which* variable is wrong, so you're guessing at what to print. In those situations, `breakpoint()` lets you pause once, at the right spot, and then look at anything you want interactively. There's no rerun because you forgot to print one more variable.

sections.heading: A General Debugging Workflow
sections.body:
Whichever tool you use, work through the same four steps:

1. **Reproduce reliably.** Before changing anything, find a way to trigger the bug consistently, ideally with the smallest input that still shows it. A bug you can't reliably trigger is a bug you can't reliably confirm you've fixed.
2. **Narrow down.** Use bisection: comment out or isolate pieces of the code, add strategic print/log statements, or use a debugger to localize where the program's behavior first diverges from what you expected. The goal is to shrink "somewhere in this 200-line module" down to "this one specific line or function."
3. **Form a hypothesis.** Once narrowed down, make a specific, falsifiable guess about the cause: not "something's probably wrong with the loop," but "I think `index` is going one past the end of the list on the last iteration." A vague hypothesis leads to vague, unproductive changes.
4. **Verify.** Test that your fix addresses the hypothesis, and that the original reproduction case no longer fails. Change one thing at a time. Fixing three suspected issues simultaneously means you won't know which one (if any) mattered, and you risk masking one bug with another.

examples.title: Reading a Traceback From the Bottom Up
examples.code:
def get_discount_rate(customer):
    return customer["discount_rate"]

def apply_discount(price, customer):
    rate = get_discount_rate(customer)
    return price * (1 - rate)

def checkout(cart_total, customer):
    return apply_discount(cart_total, customer)

checkout(100, {"name": "Amy"})

# (Python 3.11+ also underlines part of each line with ~~~^^^; omitted here)
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "shop.py", line 11, in <module>
#     checkout(100, {"name": "Amy"})
#   File "shop.py", line 9, in checkout
#     return apply_discount(cart_total, customer)
#   File "shop.py", line 5, in apply_discount
#     rate = get_discount_rate(customer)
#   File "shop.py", line 2, in get_discount_rate
#     return customer["discount_rate"]
# KeyError: 'discount_rate'
examples.explanation: Reading from the bottom up: the last line, `KeyError: 'discount_rate'`, is the exception: some dictionary lookup for the key `'discount_rate'` failed. The frame above it shows where: line 2, inside get_discount_rate, on `customer["discount_rate"]`. That tells you *where* it crashed. But the *why* is further up: apply_discount called get_discount_rate with a customer dict that never had a `'discount_rate'` key. Looking at the very top frame, the caller passed `{"name": "Amy"}`, a dict with no discount_rate at all. The fix likely isn't inside get_discount_rate (e.g. defensively using `.get("discount_rate", 0)` might just hide the problem). The useful question is why a customer record without a discount rate ever reached checkout().

examples.title: Pausing With breakpoint() Instead of Guessing With print()
examples.code:
def calculate_total(items):
    subtotal = sum(item["price"] for item in items)
    breakpoint()
    discount = subtotal * 0.1 if subtotal > 100 else 0
    return subtotal - discount

calculate_total([{"price": 60}, {"price": 70}])

# At the breakpoint, an interactive session opens (pdb's location lines omitted):
# (Pdb) p subtotal
# 130
# (Pdb) n
# (Pdb) n            <- needed on 3.13+, which stops on the breakpoint() line itself
# (Pdb) p discount
# 13.0
# (Pdb) c
# (program continues to completion)
examples.explanation: Instead of guessing in advance which variables might matter and sprinkling print(subtotal) and print(discount) through the function ahead of time, breakpoint() pauses execution each time that line is reached and hands control to an interactive session. `p subtotal` inspects the current value of subtotal on demand (130, confirming the sum is correct), then `n` runs the discount line (from Python 3.13 it takes two: the debugger stops on the breakpoint() line itself, where earlier versions stopped on the line after), letting `p discount` check the computed discount (13.0) right after it's calculated, without having decided beforehand that this was the variable to check. `c` resumes normal execution to completion. If a value turns out to be wrong, you can also just try expressions live at the prompt (e.g. `p subtotal * 0.1`) to test a fix before touching the source file.

misconceptions.description: The top line of a traceback tells you where the bug is, since that's where the program started running and reading top-to-bottom is the natural order.
misconceptions.clarification: The top of a traceback is almost always the least specific, least actionable line, typically just the entry point (like the line that called your main function), which you already know about. The most immediately useful information is at the bottom: the exception type and message, and the exact line where it was raised. That said, the bottom-most frame tells you *where* the program crashed, which is not automatically the same as *why*. The value that caused the crash may have been handed down from a caller several frames higher up, so after starting at the bottom, you often need to walk upward through the frames above it to find the root cause, rather than assuming the crash site is where the mistake lives.
misconceptions.fact: The top of a traceback is almost always the least specific, least actionable line, typically just the entry point (like the line that called your main function), which you already know about.

misconceptions.description: Interactive debuggers like pdb are heavyweight tools for advanced developers or large codebases -- print statements are always simpler and faster for everyday bugs.
misconceptions.clarification: breakpoint() requires no imports, no setup, and no extra tooling. It's a built-in function you can drop into any line of any script, and it's often faster than the print-edit-rerun cycle, not slower, once a bug requires inspecting more than one or two variables or is buried inside a loop or a conditionally-reached branch. print-debugging is fine for quick, narrow, deterministic checks, but it isn't automatically the faster or simpler option in every case; interactive stepping and inspection frequently save time compared to repeatedly guessing what to print next and restarting the whole program to check.

exercises.prompt: Running this code raises the traceback shown in the comment. Use the traceback to find where the bug actually needs to be fixed, and correct it.
hints: The bottom frame shows where the crash happened. But ask yourself whether average() itself is where the bug should be fixed, or whether it's just where a bad input finally caused a visible crash.
Walk up one frame: which student's score list caused len(numbers) to be zero?
Decide what SHOULD happen for a student with no scores at all. Should average() guess, or should the caller avoid calling it that way, or both?
exercises.solutionExplanation: The traceback's bottom frame shows the crash happening inside average(), at sum(numbers) / len(numbers), and that's where the ZeroDivisionError is raised, because Ben's score list is empty and len([]) is 0. But walking up one frame shows what happened: summarize_scores() is calling average() once per student with whatever list happens to be in scores_by_student, including a student with no scores recorded. The fix has to decide what an average of zero scores should even mean. There's no mathematically correct answer, so the sensible choice is for average() to handle the empty case (returning None here, though a project might choose 0 or raise a more descriptive error depending on what callers need) rather than letting an empty list crash deep inside a division. Note that catching the ZeroDivisionError inside average() and returning 0 would hide which students had no scores at all, which could be a worse outcome than a clear None.

exercises.prompt:
You're debugging a function that computes a shopping cart's final price, and for some carts the discount comes out negative -- which should never happen. The bug seems to depend on the specific mix of items, so print statements added at the top and bottom of the function haven't pinned it down yet. Rewrite the function below to insert a breakpoint() right before the discount calculation, so you can interactively inspect `subtotal` and `member_discount_rate` at the moment they're used.

```python
def final_price(items, member_discount_rate):
    subtotal = sum(item["price"] for item in items)
    discount = subtotal * member_discount_rate
    return subtotal - discount
```
hints: breakpoint() needs no import in modern Python. It can be placed on its own line anywhere you want execution to pause.

Place it AFTER subtotal is computed but BEFORE the discount line runs, so both subtotal and member_discount_rate are already available to inspect, but discount isn't yet computed from possibly-bad inputs.
Once paused, `p member_discount_rate` would immediately reveal if a caller passed something unexpected, like a value greater than 1 or a negative number.
exercises.solutionCode:
def final_price(items, member_discount_rate):
    subtotal = sum(item["price"] for item in items)
    breakpoint()
    discount = subtotal * member_discount_rate
    return subtotal - discount
exercises.solutionExplanation: Placing breakpoint() right after subtotal is computed, but before discount is calculated, pauses execution at the moment where both suspect inputs (subtotal and member_discount_rate) are available to inspect, but before the (possibly buggy) calculation that uses them has run. From the interactive prompt, `p member_discount_rate` would immediately show whether a caller is passing something unexpected (for instance, a negative rate, or a rate greater than 1 meant to be a percentage like 20 instead of 0.2), which prints at the top and bottom of the function would miss, since neither shows the rate where it's used.

assessments.prompt: A traceback's bottom-most frame shows a TypeError raised inside a small utility function that adds two numbers together. What is the most accurate description of what that bottom frame tells you?
options: It is irrelevant, since only the top frame of a traceback matters for debugging.
It proves the bug is inside the utility function itself, and the fix should always be made there.
It means the utility function should be rewritten to catch and silence all exceptions.
It tells you exactly where the exception was raised, but the root cause -- such as a caller passing the wrong kind of value -- may lie in a different frame further up the stack.
assessments.explanation: The bottom frame reliably tells you WHERE an exception was raised, but not necessarily WHY the bad value existed in the first place. That often traces back to a caller further up the stack that supplied an unexpected type or value. The “It proves the bug is inside…” option overstates what the crash site alone proves; a defensive fix inside the utility function might just hide a bug that originates elsewhere. The “It is irrelevant, since only the top…” option has the reading order backwards. The bottom, not the top, is where the most specific, actionable information lives. The “It means the utility function should…” option describes actively hiding failures rather than debugging them, which tends to convert a loud, traceable crash into a much harder-to-find silent bug later.

assessments.prompt: You're handed a bug report: "the export feature sometimes produces a corrupted file, but only for some users, and I can't tell why." Walk through how you'd approach this using the reproduce / narrow down / hypothesize / verify workflow, and explain where breakpoint() versus print() would each be more useful.
assessments.modelAnswer: First, reproduce reliably: try to find a specific input or user account that triggers the corruption consistently, rather than working from a vague "sometimes". This might mean asking the reporting user for their exact data, or writing a script that generates many export scenarios until one reliably fails. Without a repeatable trigger, you can't confirm a fix worked versus the bug just not showing up this time. Second, narrow down: isolate which stage of the export pipeline first produces bad output. If the pipeline reads data, transforms it, and writes a file, check the data right after each stage rather than only at the very end, to figure out which specific stage is where correct data first becomes incorrect. For a straightforward, narrow check like "is this one specific value already wrong right after step 2," a quick print() might be enough. But if the corruption seems to depend on a particular combination of several fields, or only shows up after many loop iterations, breakpoint() is more efficient. You can pause once inside the loop, inspect several related variables interactively without having predicted in advance which ones to print, and step forward iteration by iteration until the exact moment something goes wrong. Third, form a specific hypothesis once narrowed down (e.g. "I think a certain character encoding is being mishandled for names containing non-ASCII characters"), rather than a vague "something about international users." Finally, verify: confirm the fix addresses that hypothesis, and rerun the original reliable reproduction case to make sure it no longer corrupts the file, rather than assuming the bug is gone because the complaints stopped.

assessments.prompt: You're paused in the debugger inside a function called outer(), and the current line (the one about to run) calls helper(). Which pdb command steps execution INTO helper() so you can inspect what happens inside it, line by line, rather than running it to completion in one jump?
options: l (list)
s (step)
n (next)
c (continue)
assessments.explanation: `s` (step) follows execution into a function call, pausing again at the very first line inside it, which is what's needed to inspect helper()'s internals. `n` (next) does the opposite for a call on the current line: it runs the whole called function to completion in one jump and pauses again only once control returns to the current function, without stopping anywhere inside the callee. `c` (continue) runs until the next breakpoint or program end, skipping far more than just one function call. `l` (list) only shows the surrounding source code. It doesn't affect execution at all.

concepts.title: Git and GitHub
concepts.description: Git tracks snapshots of a project over time and lets you branch, commit, and merge work safely; GitHub adds a shared remote copy and a pull-request workflow on top of that same local model.
learningObjectives: Explain git's snapshot-based mental model, as distinct from tracking diffs.
Describe the local workflow of staging and committing changes.
Explain why a git branch is a lightweight, cheap pointer rather than a full copy of the project.
Distinguish a local repository from a remote (e.g. GitHub) one, and describe how they relate via push and pull.
Describe a typical feature workflow: branch, commit, push, pull request -- and explain what .gitignore is for.

sections.heading: What Git Actually Tracks: Snapshots, Not Diffs
sections.body: You might assume git stores, for each commit, only what changed since the previous one. Its model is different: **each commit is a complete snapshot of your whole project's tracked files at that point in time**. Git is efficient about this internally (unchanged files between commits aren't duplicated on disk, since commits that share content share the same underlying stored objects, and packfiles compress similar objects against each other), but every commit still represents the whole project. Two consequences: checking out an old commit gives you the *whole* project as it was, and comparing two arbitrary commits, even ones far apart in history, compares two complete snapshots. (`git show` and `git log -p` display diffs, but git computes those on demand.)

sections.heading: The Local Workflow: Stage, Then Commit
sections.body: Day-to-day git work happens in two steps. `git add <file>` (or `git add .` for everything) moves changes into the **staging area** (also called the index), a holding area where you assemble the set of changes you want to bundle into the next commit. `git commit -m "message"` then takes whatever is currently staged and seals it into a permanent snapshot in the project's history, with that message attached. Having two steps lets you be selective: if you've been working on two unrelated things, you can stage and commit one of them and leave the other for a later commit. `git status` at any point shows you what's staged, what's changed but not staged, and what git isn't tracking at all yet.

sections.heading: Branches Are Lightweight Pointers, Not Copies
sections.body: A branch may look like a separate, full copy of the project. In git, it is only a small, movable pointer (technically a reference, usually a tiny file containing a commit's hash) that says "this branch currently points at this specific commit." Creating a new branch (`git branch feature-x` or `git switch -c feature-x`) is close to instantaneous because it isn't copying anything. It's just writing one new pointer that happens to point at the same commit your current branch is already pointing at. As you commit new work while on that branch, only that branch's pointer moves forward to follow the new commits; other branches' pointers stay where they were. Creating a branch to try something out, and deleting it if it doesn't pan out, costs almost nothing.

sections.heading: Local Repository vs. Remote (GitHub)
sections.body: A git repository (the full commit history, all branches, everything) lives, complete, on your own machine the moment you run `git init` or `git clone`; git is fundamentally a *distributed* version control system, meaning there's no requirement to talk to a server for most operations. GitHub (and similar services like GitLab or Bitbucket) is a **remote**: another copy of that same repository, hosted elsewhere, that your local repository can be configured to talk to. `git push` sends commits from your local branch up to the corresponding branch on the remote; `git pull` (roughly, fetch + merge) brings commits that exist on the remote down into your local repository. This separation matters: you can commit, branch, view history, and undo changes offline, with zero network access, because all of that only touches your local repository. Only operations like clone, fetch, pull, and push need to reach GitHub.

sections.heading: A Typical Feature Workflow, and .gitignore
sections.body:
A common day-to-day flow for adding a feature looks like: create a new branch off of the main branch (`git switch -c add-login-page`), make changes and commit them locally as you go, `git push` that branch up to GitHub, then open a **pull request** (a GitHub-specific concept, not a git one), proposing that your branch's changes be reviewed and merged into `main`. Once approved, the pull request is merged, folding your branch's commits into `main` on the remote, and everyone else's local repositories can then `git pull` to catch up.

Separately, a `.gitignore` file tells git which files or patterns to never track at all: build artifacts (compiled output, `__pycache__/`), editor and OS clutter (`.DS_Store`, `.vscode/`), and anything containing secrets (API keys, passwords, `.env` files with credentials). Take the last category seriously: once a secret is committed, it exists in your project's history permanently, on every clone, even if you delete the file and commit that deletion afterward. Removing it from history for good requires actively rewriting history (and, more importantly, rotating/revoking the leaked credential itself, since you should assume anything ever committed and pushed may have been seen). Set up `.gitignore` *before* you start committing. It has no effect on files git already tracks; for those, run `git rm --cached <file>` first.

examples.title: Staging Selectively Before Committing
examples.code:
# working directory has two unrelated changes:
#   - a bug fix in auth.py
#   - unrelated, half-finished experimentation in scratch.py

# $ git status
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   modified:   auth.py
#   modified:   scratch.py

# stage and commit ONLY the finished, related change:
# $ git add auth.py
# $ git commit -m "Fix session timeout bug in login flow"

# $ git status
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   modified:   scratch.py
examples.explanation: Even though both files were modified in the working directory, `git add auth.py` stages only that one file into the index, and the subsequent `git commit` seals a snapshot in which auth.py is updated and scratch.py is the same as in the previous commit. scratch.py's modifications are left completely untouched, still sitting as unstaged changes afterward. The staging area lets you build a commit that represents one describable change ("fix session timeout bug") while unrelated edits are still in progress. To split changes within a single file, use `git add -p`.

examples.title: Creating a Branch Doesn't Copy Anything
examples.code:
# $ git log --oneline
# a1b2c3d (HEAD -> main) Add user profile page

# $ git switch -c add-search-feature
# Switched to a new branch 'add-search-feature'

# $ git log --oneline
# a1b2c3d (HEAD -> add-search-feature, main) Add user profile page

# both 'main' and 'add-search-feature' point at the SAME commit right now

# $ echo 'def search(): pass' >> search.py
# $ git add search.py
# $ git commit -m "Add search stub"

# $ git log --oneline
# 9f8e7d6 (HEAD -> add-search-feature) Add search stub
# a1b2c3d (main) Add user profile page

# only add-search-feature's pointer moved forward; main is untouched
examples.explanation: Right after `git switch -c add-search-feature`, both branch names point at the exact same commit (a1b2c3d). Creating the branch didn't duplicate any files or history, it just added a second named pointer alongside the existing one. Committing new work while on add-search-feature moves only that branch's pointer forward to the new commit (9f8e7d6); main's pointer is left where it was, still pointing at a1b2c3d. This is why switching back to main at this point would show the project without the search stub at all: main's snapshot hasn't changed, since nothing has been done to move its pointer.

misconceptions.description: Creating a new git branch makes a full copy of the entire project, so having many branches around uses a lot of extra disk space and takes real time to set up.
misconceptions.clarification: A branch is a small pointer (a reference to a specific commit), not a copy of the project's files. Creating one is close to instantaneous and takes essentially no extra disk space, because it isn't duplicating any content. It's just recording "this name points at this commit," initially the same commit your current branch already points at. It can look like a full copy because switching branches rewrites the files in your working directory, but git is only writing out a snapshot it already has stored.
misconceptions.fact: A branch is a small pointer (a reference to a specific commit), not a copy of the project's files.

misconceptions.description: A local git repository and its GitHub remote are essentially the same thing -- as long as you've pushed at some point, they're always in sync automatically.
misconceptions.clarification: They are two separate, independent copies of the repository's history that only synchronize when you run `git push` or `git pull` (or `git fetch`). Committing locally does not automatically appear on GitHub, and someone else's commits pushed to GitHub do not automatically appear in your local repository. You can commit many times locally, offline, and GitHub won't reflect any of it until you push. So two collaborators can end up with diverging histories that need a pull (and possibly a merge) to reconcile.

exercises.prompt: Given this sequence of commands, what will `git status` report right before the last line runs, and why?
exercises.code:
$ git init
$ echo "print('hello')" > app.py
$ git add app.py
$ git commit -m "Initial commit"
$ echo "print('goodbye')" >> app.py
$ git status
hints: The commit already happened before app.py was changed again. Does committing 'freeze' a file against all future edits, or just record its state at that moment?
The second echo command appends a new line to app.py AFTER the commit. Has that new change been staged with git add yet?
git status distinguishes three states: untracked, modified-but-unstaged, and staged. Which one applies to a tracked file that's been edited again since its last commit, but not yet re-added?
exercises.expectedAnswer: git status will report app.py as modified but not staged for commit. The commit captured app.py's content at that moment; the later append to the file changes its content again, and since git add was never run a second time, that new change sits as an unstaged modification. It is not automatically included in any commit.
exercises.solutionExplanation: git commit only ever seals whatever is currently staged. It has no ongoing effect on the file afterward. Once "Initial commit" is made, app.py is committed as it existed at that moment. The next line appends a new print statement to app.py, which changes the file's content on disk, but since git add app.py is never run again after that edit, the change is not staged. git status therefore reports app.py under 'Changes not staged for commit'. Git has noticed the file differs from its last committed snapshot, but the new content hasn't been added to the index yet, so a git commit run at this point would not include it.

exercises.prompt: A developer accidentally committed and pushed a file containing a real API key because their project had no .gitignore. Given the commands below that led to the mistake, identify what should have been done differently and fix the setup going forward.
exercises.code:
$ git init
$ echo "API_KEY=sk-real-secret-value-123" > .env
$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Initial commit"
$ git push origin main
hints: The root problem happened at `git add .`. It staged EVERY file in the directory, including one that should never have been tracked in the first place.
A .gitignore file, created and committed before ever running git add on a secret-containing file, would have excluded it from being staged at all.

Fixing the setup for next time is not the same as fully undoing a leak that already happened. Once pushed, the secret should also be treated as compromised and rotated, not just removed from future commits.
exercises.solutionCode:
$ git init
$ echo ".env" > .gitignore
$ git add .gitignore
$ git commit -m "Add .gitignore"

# now .env is safely ignored going forward:
$ echo "API_KEY=sk-real-secret-value-123" > .env
$ git add .
$ git status
# .env does NOT appear -- git ignores it entirely, so it's never staged or committed

# NOTE: this only prevents FUTURE leaks. Since the real key was already
# pushed in the scenario above, it must also be revoked/rotated at the
# provider -- removing it from a later commit does not erase it from history
# that's already been pushed and potentially cloned or cached elsewhere.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The mistake happened at `git add .`, which stages every file in the working directory indiscriminately, including .env. There was nothing telling git to treat that file specially. Creating a .gitignore file listing .env, and committing that .gitignore before ever staging the secret file, means a later `git add .` will skip .env. Git status won't even list it as untracked, because .gitignore tells git to ignore it. This only protects against future leaks; it does nothing to erase the secret that was already committed and pushed in the original scenario, since that commit already exists in history and may already have been fetched by anyone with access to the remote. And in a repository where .env is already tracked, .gitignore alone won't stop git from tracking it: run `git rm --cached .env` and commit that too. The only fully safe response to an already-leaked credential is to treat it as compromised and rotate/revoke it at the source (e.g. generate a new API key and invalidate the old one). Deleting the file in a new commit leaves the old value fully readable in the repository's history.

assessments.prompt: What is the most accurate description of what a git branch actually is?
options: A remote-only concept that doesn't exist until you push to GitHub.
A full, separate copy of every file in the project at the time the branch was created.
A folder inside the .git directory containing a duplicate of the project's entire history.
A lightweight, movable pointer to a specific commit.
assessments.explanation: A branch is a small reference, essentially a name pointing at a commit's hash, not a copy of files or history. Creating one is cheap because it involves no duplication: it just adds a new pointer, initially aimed at the same commit as whatever branch you created it from. As you commit while that branch is checked out, only its pointer advances to follow the new commits. The “A full, separate copy of every file…” and “A folder inside the .git directory containing…” options describe a copying behavior that git avoids for performance and simplicity. The “A remote-only concept that doesn't exist until…” option is wrong because branches are a core local git concept. They exist and work fully offline, independent of GitHub or any remote.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to someone who has only used a tool like Google Docs' version history, how git's local-repository-plus-remote model differs from a single shared online document, and why that difference matters for collaboration.
assessments.modelAnswer: In something like Google Docs, there's essentially one authoritative copy of the document living on a server, and every edit you make is sent there more or less immediately. There isn't a meaningful separate 'your own copy' that exists independently. Git works differently: a full, complete repository (every commit, every branch, the whole history) lives on your own machine the moment you clone or initialize it, and you can commit, create branches, inspect history, and even undo changes offline, because none of that touches any server at all. GitHub (or another host) holds a separate copy of that same repository, and the two only synchronize when you push (send your local commits up) or pull (bring the remote's commits down). There's no automatic, continuous syncing happening in the background. This matters for collaboration because it means multiple people can work independently, each accumulating their own local commits, without needing constant connectivity or fear of instantly overwriting each other's in-progress work the way simultaneous edits to a single live document might collide. The tradeoff is that reconciling everyone's independent work requires extra steps (pushing, pulling, and sometimes merging), rather than it happening automatically and invisibly, and pull requests give that step a place for review before changes land on a shared branch like main.

assessments.prompt: Developer A makes three commits locally but never runs git push. Developer B clones the project from GitHub right now. Which of A's three local commits will B's clone contain?
options: Only the first of the three, since git automatically pushes the earliest unpushed commit after a period of inactivity
All three, since git automatically syncs local commits to GitHub in the background as they're made
None of them -- since A never pushed, GitHub's copy (and therefore B's fresh clone, which comes from GitHub) has no knowledge of any of A's three local commits
It depends on whether B's clone command includes a special synchronization flag
assessments.explanation: A local repository and its GitHub remote only synchronize through commands (push and pull (or fetch)), never automatically or in the background. A's three commits exist only in A's local repository until A pushes them. Since that push never happened, GitHub's copy of the repository is completely unaware any of those commits exist, and B's clone, which copies from GitHub, naturally contains none of them either. The commits don't exist anywhere outside A's machine yet.
